menu_items.name: Shin Ramyun Original — Single Pack
menu_items.description: The beef-and-mushroom broth that made Korean instant noodles famous, with a clean chilli burn that builds as you eat.
menu_items.short_description: The beef-and-mushroom broth that made Korean instant noodles famous, with a clean chilli burn that builds as you eat.
menu_items.long_description: Shin Ramyun has been Korea's best selling instant noodle since 1986, and it is the pack most people mean when they say Korean ramyun. The broth is built on beef and shiitake with a clean gochugaru burn that hits the back of the throat rather than the tongue, and the noodles are thick enough to stay springy right to the bottom of the bowl. It carries around 3,400 Scoville units, which is hot but not punishing.
menu_items.serving_suggestion: Boil 550ml of water, add the noodles and both sachets, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes. Crack an egg in during the last minute and finish with spring onion.
menu_items.ingredients: Wheat flour, palm oil, potato starch, modified potato starch, salt, hydrolysed soy protein, red chilli pepper, garlic, shiitake mushroom extract, beef bone extract, black pepper, dried spring onion, dried carrot, dried shiitake mushroom.
menu_items.allergens: Contains wheat, soy and beef. May contain milk, egg and fish.

menu_items.name: Shin Ramyun Black — Single Pack
menu_items.description: The premium Shin, with an added beef bone broth sachet that turns the soup milky and full-bodied.
menu_items.short_description: The premium Shin, with an added beef bone broth sachet that turns the soup milky and full-bodied.
menu_items.long_description: Shin Black adds a second sachet of seolleongtang, the slow simmered ox bone broth Koreans eat for breakfast, on top of the standard Shin base. The result is milkier, rounder and noticeably less sharp than the red pack, with sliced shiitake, bok choy and roasted garlic in the vegetable mix. The noodles are thicker too, so it eats more like a restaurant bowl than an instant one.
menu_items.serving_suggestion: Cook in 550ml of water for 4 to 5 minutes, then stir the seolleongtang sachet in off the heat so the broth stays milky.

menu_items.short_description: Seafood noodle soup in the Korean-Chinese style, with squid and vegetable flakes in a peppery red broth.
menu_items.long_description: Champong is the Korean-Chinese seafood noodle soup you get from takeaway shops, and this is Nongshim's version of it. menu_items.long_description: Champong is the Korean-Chinese seafood noodle soup you get from takeaway shops, and this is Nongshim's version of it. The broth is smoky and peppery rather than sweet, built from cuttlefish, mussel, scallop, shrimp and crab with a red chilli oil finish. Cabbage, bok choy and seaweed flakes rehydrate into something closer to a restaurant bowl than most instant seafood packs manage.
menu_items.serving_suggestion: Cook in 550ml of water for 4 to 5 minutes. A handful of prawns or mussels dropped in at the start turns it into a proper meal.
menu_items.ingredients: Enriched wheat flour, potato starch, palm oil, modified potato starch, dried vegetable flakes (cabbage, bok choy, red chilli, mushroom, seaweed), seasoned oil (corn oil, canola oil, chilli pepper, garlic), cuttlefish extract, mussel extract, shrimp extract, crab extract, beef bone extract, salt, maltodextrin.
menu_items.allergens: Contains wheat, soy, sesame, crab and shrimp. May contain milk, egg, fish, tree nuts and peanuts.

menu_items.short_description: Korea's take on jjajangmyeon, built on a roasted black bean sauce. Savoury, mildly sweet, no chilli at all.

A roasted black bean sauce coats thick noodles with dried onion, cabbage and soy protein pieces, finished with a sachet of olive oil that lifts the whole thing. Completely free of chilli, which makes it the safe order for children and anyone who has been defeated by fire noodles.

menu_items.short_description: A soybean paste broth that is thicker and earthier than the usual chilli-forward ramyun. Mild and hearty.
menu_items.long_description: Named after the town of Anseong and on shelves since 1983, Ansungtangmyun is the doenjang pack. Fermented soybean paste and beef stock give it an earthy, almost miso-like depth that is thicker and rounder than the chilli-forward ramyun most people start with. There is warmth rather than heat, which makes it the one to reach for when you want comfort instead of a challenge.
